apmo-2024-01.title: Two homotheties and the radical axis
apmo-2024-01.body:
The line $XY$ is the radical axis of the circles $(BQX)$ and $(CPX)$. Let line $AX$ meet segment $DE$ at $Z'$ and segment $BC$ at $Z$ ($X$ is inside the trapezoid, so ray $AX$ crosses $DE$ and then $BC$). It suffices to show that $Z$ lies on the radical axis: then the radical axis is the line $XZ=AX$, which contains $A$ and $Y$.

* The homothety with centre $A$ taking line $DE$ to line $BC$ maps $D\mapsto B$, $E\mapsto C$, $Z'\mapsto Z$, so $\dfrac{BZ}{ZC}=\dfrac{DZ'}{Z'E}$.
* $X$ lies between the parallel lines $DE$ and $BC$, so the homothety with centre $X$ taking line $DE$ to line $BC$ has negative ratio and maps $D\mapsto P$, $E\mapsto Q$, $Z'\mapsto Z$. Hence $\dfrac{PZ}{ZQ}=\dfrac{DZ'}{Z'E}$, $Z$ lies between $P$ and $Q$, and $P$ is on the opposite side of line $AX$ from $D$, i.e. on the side of $C$.

Similarly $Q$ is on the side of $B$. So on line $BC$ the points $B,Q$ lie on one side of $Z$ and $P,C$ on the other, and $\frac{BZ}{ZC}=\frac{PZ}{ZQ}$ gives $ZB\cdot ZQ=ZC\cdot ZP$; as signed products both are positive, so they are equal also with signs. Line $BC$ meets circle $(BQX)$ at $B,Q$ and circle $(CPX)$ at $C,P$, so these products are the powers of $Z$ with respect to the two circles. Hence $Z$ lies on the radical axis, and $A$, $X$, $Y$ are collinear. ∎

apmo-2024-01.title: Power of $A$ via circle $DEX$
apmo-2024-01.body:
Let circle $(BQX)$ meet line $AB$ again at $S$ and circle $(CPX)$ meet line $AC$ again at $T$. With directed angles, using $DE\parallel BC$ and the circle $BQXS$:
$$\angle(ED,EX)=\angle(QB,QX)=\angle(SB,SX)=\angle(SD,SX),$$
so $S$ lies on circle $(DEX)$; similarly so does $T$. The power of $A$ with respect to $(DEX)$ gives $AS\cdot AD=AT\cdot AE$ (signed). Since $DE\parallel BC$, $\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{AE}{AC}$, and dividing, $AS\cdot AB=AT\cdot AC$. These are the powers of $A$ with respect to $(BQX)$ and $(CPX)$, so $A$ lies on their radical axis $XY$. ∎

apmo-2024-02.title: Outer coordinates and two-move shifts
apmo-2024-02.body:
Call a coordinate value $x\in\{1,\dots,100\}$ *outer* if $x\le100-k$ or $x\ge k+1$, and *central* if $101-k\le x\le k$. A coordinate can change by $k$ only if it is outer (if $x\le100-k$ only $x+k$ is in range, if $x\ge k+1$ only $x-k$), and then it stays outer. Let $x^*$ denote $x+k$ or $x-k$ accordingly; $x\mapsto x^*$ is a bijection of the outer values.

**Unreachable cells.** Every move changes one coordinate by $k$. So from a cell of the central square $S=\{(x,y): x,y \text{ central}\}$ no move is possible; since moves are reversible, no move leads into $S$ either. $S$ has side $2k-100$, and $(1,1)\notin S$. If $k$ is odd, every move changes $x+y$ by $\pm1\pm k$, an even number, so only cells with $x+y$ even can be reached.

**Two-move shifts.** If $x$ is outer, $(x,y)\to(x^*,y\pm1)\to(x,y\pm2)$, so from $(x,y)$ we reach every $(x,y')$ with $y'\equiv y\pmod 2$; and the single move $(x,y)\to(x^*,y\pm1)$ is always available (one of $y\pm1$ is in range). By the symmetry of the moves, the same holds with the roles of the coordinates exchanged.

**Reaching cells.** Since $y=1$ is outer, row $1$ gives $(x,1)$ for all odd $x$. From $(x-1,1)$ the move to $(x,1+k)$ gives $(x,1+k)$ for all even $x$. Now let $x$ be outer:
* $x$ odd: from $(x,1)$ we reach $(x,y)$ for all odd $y$;
* $x$ even: from $(x,1+k)$ we reach $(x,y)$ for all $y\equiv1+k\pmod2$.

By the symmetry, for outer $y$: $(x,y)$ is reachable for odd $x$ if $y$ is odd, and for $x\equiv1+k$ if $y$ is even.

* **$k$ odd:** this gives, for $x$ outer or $y$ outer, every cell with $x+y$ even. So the reachable cells are exactly the cells of the colour of $(1,1)$ outside $S$. Both the board and $S$ (even side) contain equally many cells of each colour, so $L(k)=\frac{100^2-(2k-100)^2}{2}$.
* **$k$ even:** for outer $x$ we get all $(x,y)$ with $y$ odd; applying $(x,y)\to(x^*,y\pm1)$ gives all $(x^*,y')$ with $y'$ even, and $x^*$ runs over all outer values. So every cell with an outer $x$ — and symmetrically with an outer $y$ — is reachable: all cells outside $S$, and $L(k)=100^2-(2k-100)^2$. ∎

apmo-2024-03.title: A two-variable lemma and telescoping
apmo-2024-03.body:
**Lemma.** For a positive integer $k$ and $x,y>0$,
$$\Bigl(\frac2{1+x}\Bigr)^{2^k}+\Bigl(\frac2{1+y}\Bigr)^{2^k}\ge2\Bigl(\frac2{1+xy}\Bigr)^{2^{k-1}} .$$

*$k=1$:* the claim is $\frac1{(1+x)^2}+\frac1{(1+y)^2}\ge\frac1{1+xy}$. Clearing denominators, it is equivalent to
$$(1+xy)\bigl((1+x)^2+(1+y)^2\bigr)-(1+x)^2(1+y)^2=xy(x-y)^2+(xy-1)^2\ge0,$$
where the identity is checked by expanding both sides.

*$k\ge2$:* let $A=\bigl(\frac2{1+x}\bigr)^{2^{k-1}}$, $B=\bigl(\frac2{1+y}\bigr)^{2^{k-1}}$. By $2(A^2+B^2)\ge(A+B)^2$ and the case $k-1$ ($A+B\ge2\bigl(\frac2{1+xy}\bigr)^{2^{k-2}}>0$),
$$2(A^2+B^2)\ge(A+B)^2\ge4\Bigl(\frac2{1+xy}\Bigr)^{2^{k-1}},$$
which is the claim. $\square$

**Telescoping.** Let $P_j=a_ja_{j+1}\cdots a_n$ and $P_{n+1}=1$. We show by downward induction on $j=n+1,n,\dots,1$:
$$\sum_{i=j}^n\frac1{2^i}\Bigl(\frac2{1+a_i}\Bigr)^{2^i}+\frac1{2^n}\ \ge\ \frac1{2^{j-1}}\Bigl(\frac2{1+P_j}\Bigr)^{2^{j-1}} .$$
For $j=n+1$ both sides equal $\frac1{2^n}$ (as $\frac2{1+P_{n+1}}=1$). If it holds for $j+1$, then by the lemma with $k=j$, $x=a_j$, $y=P_{j+1}$:
$$\sum_{i=j}^n\cdots+\frac1{2^n}\ge\frac1{2^j}\Bigl(\frac2{1+a_j}\Bigr)^{2^j}+\frac1{2^j}\Bigl(\frac2{1+P_{j+1}}\Bigr)^{2^j}\ge\frac{2}{2^j}\Bigl(\frac2{1+a_jP_{j+1}}\Bigr)^{2^{j-1}}=\frac1{2^{j-1}}\Bigl(\frac2{1+P_j}\Bigr)^{2^{j-1}} .$$
For $j=1$ this is $\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{2^i}\bigl(\frac2{1+a_i}\bigr)^{2^i}+\frac1{2^n}\ge\frac2{1+a_1\cdots a_n}$, the desired inequality. (Equality holds when all $a_i=1$.) ∎

apmo-2024-04.title: Binary digits and an inductive matching
apmo-2024-04.body:
Let $S(x)$ be the set of positions of the $1$-bits of $x$ and $s(x)=|S(x)|$. By Lucas' theorem, $\binom Nm$ is odd iff $S(m)\subseteq S(N)$. For $m<N$ this inclusion is strict, so $s(m)\le s(N)-1$. Note $S(2x)=S(x)+1$ and $S(2x+1)=\{0\}\cup(S(x)+1)$.

**Bit count.** $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}s(t+i)=t+\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}s(2i).$ Indeed $\sum_{j=0}^{2t-1}s(j)=\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\bigl(s(2j)+s(2j+1)\bigr)=2\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}s(j)+t$; subtracting $\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}s(j)$ and using $s(2j)=s(j)$ gives the claim.

**Necessary form.** Let $(a_i)$ be a valid permutation. Then $\binom{t+i}{2a_i}\ne0$ and $2a_i\ne t+i$ give $2a_i<t+i$, so $s(2a_i)\le s(t+i)-1$. Summing, and using $\sum s(2a_i)=\sum s(2i)$ (a permutation), the bit count forces equality everywhere: **$S(2a_i)$ is $S(t+i)$ with exactly one element removed**, i.e. $t+i-2a_i$ is a power of $2$ that is a $1$-bit of $t+i$. Conversely, any permutation with this property is valid.

* *$t+i$ odd.* $t+i-2a_i$ is an odd power of $2$, so it is $1$: $a_i=\frac{t+i-1}2$. Here $t+i$ runs over the odd numbers in $[t,2t-1]$, and $a_i$ over $[\lfloor t/2\rfloor,t-1]$; these choices are valid (removing bit $0$).
* *$t+i$ even,* $t+i=2m$ with $m\in B_t=[\lceil t/2\rceil,t-1]$. The remaining values form $A_t=[0,\lfloor t/2\rfloor-1]$, and $S(2a)=S(2m)$ minus one bit iff $S(a)=S(m)$ minus one bit.

So valid permutations correspond exactly to bijections $\pi:B_t\to A_t$ such that **$\pi(m)$ is $m$ with one $1$-bit deleted** (a "pairing"). It remains to prove:

**Claim.** For every $t\ge1$ there is exactly one pairing $B_t\to A_t$.

Induction on $t$. For $t\le2$: $B_1=A_1=\varnothing$; $B_2=\{1\}$, $A_2=\{0\}$. Let $t\ge3$ and let $2^a$ be the largest power of $2$ below $t$, so $2^a<t\le2^{a+1}$ and $\lceil t/2\rceil\le2^a$.

* Every $x\in[2^a,t-1]\subseteq B_t$ has bit $a$, while every element of $A_t$ is $<\lfloor t/2\rfloor\le2^a$ and lacks it. So $\pi(x)=x-2^a$ is forced, and these values fill $[0,t-1-2^a]\subseteq A_t$.
* It remains to pair $B'=[\lceil t/2\rceil,2^a-1]$ with $A'=[t-2^a,\lfloor t/2\rfloor-1]$ (equal sizes $2^a-\lceil t/2\rceil$). Let $u=2^{a+1}-t$, so $0\le u<t$, and let $c(x)=2^a-1-x$, which complements the bits in positions $0,\dots,a-1$ for $0\le x<2^a$. One computes $c(B')=[0,\lfloor u/2\rfloor-1]=A_u$ and $c(A')=[\lceil u/2\rceil,u-1]=B_u$. For $x,y<2^a$, "$y$ is $x$ with one bit deleted" iff "$c(x)$ is $c(y)$ with one bit deleted". So pairings $B'\to A'$ correspond bijectively (via $c$, swapping roles) to pairings $B_u\to A_u$, of which there is exactly one by the induction hypothesis ($u<t$; for $u=0$ both sets are empty).

Hence the pairing, and with it the permutation, exists and is unique. ∎

apmo-2024-05.title: Three Miquel points
apmo-2024-05.body:
All angles are directed angles between lines, mod $180^\circ$. We use **Miquel's theorem**: for four lines in general position, the circumcircles of the four triangles formed by three of them pass through one point (the Miquel point).

* $M$ is the Miquel point of lines $AB$, $BC$, $AD$, $\ell$ (it lies on $(PAS)$ and $(PBR)$), so it also lies on $(ABL)$ and $(LRS)$.
* $N$ is the Miquel point of lines $CD$, $BC$, $AD$, $\ell$ (on $(QCR)$, $(QDS)$), so it lies on $(LCD)$ and $(LRS)$.
* Let $E$ be the Miquel point of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$: it lies on $(KBC)$, $(KAD)$, $(LAB)$, $(LCD)$.

**$E$ lies on $t=KL$.** By the circles $KBCE$ and $LABE$ and since $ABCD$ is cyclic,
$$\angle(EK,EL)=\angle(EK,EB)+\angle(EB,EL)=\angle(CD,CB)+\angle(AB,AD)=\angle(AD,AB)+\angle(AB,AD)=0 .$$

**$M,N,P,Q$ are concyclic.** Using $(LRS)\ni M,N$, $(PAS)\ni M$, the cyclic $ABCD$, and $(QCRN)$:
$$\angle(MN,MP)=\angle(MN,MS)+\angle(MS,MP)=\angle(RN,RS)+\angle(AS,AP)=\angle(RN,RQ)+\angle(AD,AB)$$
$$=\angle(RN,RQ)+\angle(CD,CB)=\angle(RN,RQ)+\angle(CQ,CR)=\angle(RN,RQ)+\angle(NQ,NR)=\angle(QN,QR)=\angle(QN,QP),$$
where the step before last is the angle sum in triangle $NRQ$. Hence $\angle(MN,MP)=\angle(QN,QP)$.

**The circle $\omega=(EMN)$.** Let $T=NQ\cap t$ and suppose $T\ne E$. By $(LABEM)$, $(PASM)$ and $(MNQP)$:
$$\angle(ET,EM)=\angle(EL,EM)=\angle(AL,AM)=\angle(AS,AM)=\angle(PS,PM)=\angle(PQ,PM)=\angle(NQ,NM)=\angle(NT,NM),$$
so $T\in\omega$. Likewise let $V=MP\cap t$, $V\ne E$. By $(LCDEN)$, $(QDSN)$ and $(MNQP)$:
$$\angle(EV,EN)=\angle(EL,EN)=\angle(DL,DN)=\angle(DS,DN)=\angle(QS,QN)=\angle(QP,QN)=\angle(MP,MN)=\angle(MV,MN),$$
so $V\in\omega$. If $T=E$ (respectively $V=E$), the same chain reads $\angle(t,EM)=\angle(NE,NM)$ (respectively $\angle(t,EN)=\angle(ME,MN)$), which says that $t$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $E$.

**Conclusion.** $\omega$ meets the line $t$ in at most two points, one of which is $E$. If $T\ne E$ and $V\ne E$, then $T=V$. If one of them equals $E$, then $t$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $E$, so $\omega\cap t=\{E\}$ and the other one equals $E$ as well. In all cases $T=V$ is a common point of $NQ$, $MP$ and $t$, i.e. $X=T$ lies on $KL$. ∎
